approachQuestion.prompt:
Exhibit Sightline

An exhibit has n upright markers at integer positions 0 through n-1. Marker i has nonnegative integer height h[i]. Choosing i < j earns a sightline score (j-i) * min(h[i], h[j]); intermediate markers do not affect the score. Return the largest possible score, or 0 if fewer than two markers exist. Do not modify h.

Constraints: 0 <= n <= 200000; 0 <= h[i] <= 1000000000. Scores fit signed 64-bit integers; use that type for multiplication and the result.

Example 1: h = [4,1,3,2,5] -> 16, from i=0, j=4.
Example 2: h = [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7] -> 49, from i=1, j=8.
Example 3: h = [0] -> 0.
constraints: Choose the most efficient valid approach for the entire stated input domain; accept equivalent optimal variants.

options.text: Start at both ends and record the current score. Move the endpoint with smaller height inward; on equal heights move the left endpoint. Continue until the endpoints meet, returning the best score seen.
options.feedback: Once a pair is evaluated, keeping its shorter endpoint while narrowing the distance cannot improve on that pair, so that endpoint can be discarded.

options.text: Use the same endpoint scan and smaller-height rule, but on equal heights move the right endpoint instead of the left.
options.feedback: Either endpoint can be discarded on a tie: every narrower pair retaining it is capped by the same height and a smaller distance.

options.text: Copy h into a new array, then run the smaller-height endpoint scan on that copy and return its best score.
options.feedback: The score is correct, but the scan only reads heights, so the full copy is unnecessary.

options.text: Start at both ends, record each score, and always move the taller endpoint inward; on a tie move the left endpoint.
options.feedback: For [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7], it discards the final height 7 before comparing it with height 8 at index 1 and misses score 49.

feedback.reason: Prove dominance-based elimination using the limiting height and shrinking distance, even though the input is unsorted.
details: Evaluate the pair at the two current endpoints and retain its score if it is the largest seen. Discard the endpoint with the smaller height; use the left endpoint on a tie. Repeat while the endpoints differ. Return zero immediately for fewer than two markers.

With the shorter endpoint fixed, moving the opposite endpoint inward reduces width without improving the limiting height. Discard that shorter endpoint to explore pairs that can actually beat the current score.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed after question 1, choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair, with n equal to the original input length. Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed reads, writes, comparisons, and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include every temporary buffer, copy, and call frame. The fixed method is iterative, makes no input copy, uses no hashing, and performs no amortized data-structure operations. Exclude the supplied input and returned scalar; include all other storage. No recursion, slices, or allocated work arrays are used.
constraints: Choose the tightest pair for this fixed method, regardless of the approach you selected in question 1.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Each iteration permanently discards one endpoint.
details: Each iteration removes one endpoint, yielding n-1 iterations for n>=2. Each comparison and score update uses fixed work. Only two indices, a score, and the best score are retained.

Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed reads, writes, comparisons, and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include every temporary buffer, copy, and call frame. The fixed method is iterative, makes no input copy, uses no hashing, and performs no amortized data-structure operations. Exclude the supplied input and returned scalar; include all other storage. No recursion, slices, or allocated work arrays are used.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This adds a size-dependent temporary copy or buffer absent from the fixed method.
“O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The method does not restart a full scan for each element; its bounded number of forward or inward scans is linear.
“O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: No sorting or repeated binary searches occur in the fixed method.
